articles.title: This Is the Most Popular Halloween Candy in Your State
articles.content:
We all have our go-to Halloween candy. I tend to buy what I also like to eat (Reese’s, Butterfinger), but I can also see how saddling the neighborhood kids with Mounds might be tempting. It’s a little mean, but buying unpopular candy would be a great way to keep me from stuffing every bar in my mouth before the doorbell even rings once.
My mom gave out full-size Hershey bars when I was a kid, a practice she got from her mom that I continue today, though after that symbolic first box, I switch to my peanut-buttery faves. You know, just in case the ghost-and-goblin traffic is light and I end up with extras. (So sad!)
How do you pick your Halloween candy? Do you go with what’s popular, what’s cheap or whatever’s available when you race to the store to restock when the hordes are fast approaching and you just ran out of candy? Well, DoorDash decided to quantify this choice for people all across the country, and we’re bringing them to you now.
Coming up, we have the most popular Halloween candy in every state in 2026, according to real DoorDash numbers. Keep reading to see if you align with your state’s most popular candy.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more Halloween, food, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
This contest went straight to the source: DoorDash receipts. To find out which Halloween candy is the most popular in each state and across the country, DoorDash analyzed customer candy orders from last year (between Oct. 1 and Oct. 31, 2025, when everyone was stocking up on Halloween candy) to see what might be popular this year.
The results were a range of old favorites and up-and-comers that have muscled their way into top spots. Here’s the full ranking, followed by national and regional trends.
This contest wasn’t even close. Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups swept to victory in 17 states this year—that’s a full third of the country. My mom’s go-to, the Hershey bar, made the list too, along with some regional favorites and non-chocolate choices like Laffy Taffy and Sweetarts.
Here’s the most popular Halloween candy in every state, according to DoorDash.
For the third year in a row, Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups dominated the standings. And while sugary-sweet (or sour, as the case may be) gummy treats made significant strides this year, capturing five of the top 10 spots, chocolate still came out on top overall. The top four favorite Halloween candies in the U.S. are chocolate-based goodies, along with KitKat, which came in at No. 10 (but, interestingly, did not earn a state ranking).
Taking a look at the map, it’s clear that where you live matters when it comes to what you might find in your kid’s Halloween bucket this year—though we know one choice will be thoroughly represented. Reese’s has a stranglehold in New England, the Rust Belt, the Mid-Atlantic and the Pacific Northwest.
Laffy Taffy pulls most of its fans from the upper Midwest, while across the South, the private-label Sweet Smiles Candy, which is sold at Dollar Stores, dominates in seven Southern states and nowhere else. Sweetarts is popular in the Southwest states of New Mexico and Oklahoma, plus Kansas and Idaho, but is absent east of the Mississippi.
Red Vines and its licorice nemesis, Twizzlers, each bagged two states, with the iconic Vines repping the West via California and Arizona, and Twizzlers making its stand rather randomly in Wyoming and Missouri.
DoorDash reports that old-fashioned candy is making some headway this year, with the formerly dust-gathering Circus Peanuts up 350% in 2026 and Bit-O-Honey up 180%. Lemonheads, those delicious little pebbles of sour goodness, are also back: They’re up 200%. And Dum-Dums suckers aren’t just for the bank anymore, as interest doubled from last year.
Even lowly candy corn is asserting itself, possibly due to a massive publicity push by Brach’s, which includes a candy corn perfume, if you can believe it. Purchases of the love-’em-or-hate-’em striped sugar triangles are up 30% from last year. On the other end of the spectrum, my mom will be thrilled that shares of DoorDash orders with full-size candy bars grew to 20%.
Finally, the very last thing children want to discover they failed to avoid at the end of the night, the tiny box of raisins, is somehow up a rather suspicious 60%. Keep your eyes peeled this Halloween, kids, because someone out there made a big purchase.
The post This Is the Most Popular Halloween Candy in Your State appeared first on Reader's Digest.

articles.title: Here’s What Really Happens to Leaves When They Change Color in the Fall
articles.content:
There are many things to love about fall: football weekends, apple cider doughnuts, that first genuinely crisp morning when you can finally break out a sweater, and, of course, the foliage. One day, the landscape is overwhelmingly green. Then, seemingly overnight, the leaves start showing off—yellow, orange, red and even deep purple. It’s a transformation we marvel at every year, but how often do we stop to ask what’s actually happening?
It turns out that behind all that seasonal color is a carefully timed process that helps trees prepare for winter. In other words, there’s more to that fall foliage than meets the eye.
To find out what’s really happening when leaves put on their annual fall show, I spoke with Jason Grabosky, PhD, a professor in the Department of Ecology, Evolution and Natural Resources at Rutgers University, and Jessica A. Savage, PhD, an associate professor in the Department of Biology at the University of Minnesota Duluth.
Read on for the details that will make you appreciate all of those gorgeous colors even more.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Time for a quick science refresher: A leaf is green because it contains a pigment called chlorophyll. As Savage explains, that’s what helps plants capture light energy for photosynthesis, the process by which plants make sugars. Chlorophyll absorbs many wavelengths of light but reflects green, which is the color we see.
Throughout the growing season, chlorophyll is constantly made and broken down, keeping leaves green while the tree captures sunlight and produces energy. But as fall approaches, the tree changes its priorities.
As summer turns to fall, trees begin preparing for winter. One of their biggest signals is the changing amount of daylight—specifically, the increasing amount of darkness. “When the nighttime gets too long, the tree stops building that molecule because it’s expensive to build and it’s not getting the payout before it rips and breaks again,” Grabosky explains. “It’s too much work.”
As chlorophyll production slows, the green fades. But the tree isn’t simply letting the leaf go to waste. “To avoid losing all of these nutrients when leaves drop, plants reabsorb them in the autumn,” Savage says. The tree begins pulling nutrients out of its leaves and storing them in its branches and trunk, essentially giving itself a little winter savings account.
Here’s where things get colorful—and interesting. Leaves contain several pigments besides chlorophyll, including carotenoids, which produce yellow and orange hues. These pigments are present during much of the growing season but are masked by green chlorophyll. As the green fades, those yellow and orange tones become increasingly visible. So that gorgeous yellow leaf you’ve spotted in October isn’t necessarily making yellow pigment all of the sudden. In many cases, the yellow was there all along. (Bonus fun fact: One carotenoid, lutein, also causes the yellow color of egg yolks.)
Red is a little different. Red and reddish-purple colors come largely from anthocyanins, pigments that some plants produce in the fall. The right weather can help bring out those reds. “The reds are really dependent on those sunny days where [trees are] getting the energy, along with those really cool nights,” Grabosky says.
But scientists don’t think trees make anthocyanins simply to put on a good show. Savage explains that as the leaf’s chemistry changes, it may become more vulnerable to light-related damage. Anthocyanins may help shield the leaf while the tree finishes its seasonal work.
Leaves don’t necessarily follow a universal green → yellow → orange → red → brown progression. Different species have different pigments and respond differently to changing conditions. “Every species is going to be a little bit different because they’re playing the energy game to compete for light, and each has its own little niche as a species,” Grabosky says.
Some leaves turn yellow and then brown. Others develop orange or red tones. Even leaves on the same tree can vary depending on how much light they receive. Savage calls this a “mosaic of leaf colors.” In sumacs, for example, shaded portions may be less red and more orange.
Weather matters too. “If you’ve got sunny days and cool nights, you’re going to get that more vibrant color,” Grabosky says.
Eventually, the tree forms a specialized layer of cells called an abscission zone, where the leaf meets the branch. Those cells weaken the connection until the leaf can drop. So when a leaf finally flutters to the ground, it isn’t simply falling off. The tree has been carefully preparing to let it go.
They do—but not necessarily in the way we expect. Evergreens, for example, keep their leaves or needles for multiple years rather than shedding them every fall. Older needles eventually yellow and drop, but the process happens gradually within the canopy, Grabosky explains. Other trees may lose their leaves without producing brilliant fall colors. Drought, pests and other stresses can cause leaves to brown or drop early.
Some oaks and beeches even hold onto their brown leaves through winter. Grabosky says several proposed explanations include the possibility that the bitter dead leaves discourage animals from eating them and help protect next year’s buds. The leaves may also provide some insulation.
In other words, not every tree needs a dramatic fall finale.
You don’t need to live in New England to see leaves change color, but geography makes a big difference in how dramatic the show is. Trees throughout the country receive the seasonal light signal, but farther south, you never really get that vast difference in day length and temperature, Grabosky says. As you move north and higher in elevation, you’re more likely to see a dramatic fall display.
Weather can also change the show within a region. Cool nights can intensify fall colors, particularly reds, while drought can diminish the display and cause leaves to brown or drop early.
The types of trees growing in an area matter just as much. “The plants that occur in one area might be different than those that occur in another,” Savage explains. “Northern Minnesota, for example, has many sugar maples, which can produce brilliant orange and yellow foliage. Florida, meanwhile, has many plants with evergreen leaves, including live oaks and rhododendrons.”
So the spectacular foliage of the Northeast isn’t caused by one magic ingredient. “It’s a combination of the kinds of trees, the amount of darkness and the quality of the cool temperatures,” Grabosky says.
And let’s not forget about the tree’s overall health. “If you have a happy, healthy tree going into the fall, you get a better fall color,” Grabosky says. After a particularly hot or stressful year, the landscape may look different.
Climate change may be influencing the timing and intensity of fall foliage. While the seasonal light signal remains the same, says Grabosky, “if we’re having longer, milder falls, we’re going to have conditions for photosynthesis a little bit longer.” That could keep green in the landscape longer and downplay some of the reds and oranges.
Scientists are using aerial photography and satellites to track fall foliage and study how climate change is affecting the timing of plant growth around the world. Even the annual leaf-peeping season can offer clues about a changing climate.
When spring arrives, rising temperatures and longer days signal to the tree that it’s time to resume growth. Interestingly, many trees produce young leaves inside buds during the summer—yes, right before fall. “These leaves remain dormant all winter, and in the spring when the buds open, they expand,” Savage says.
At first, the developing leaves rely on sugars that the tree stored the previous year. Then the new leaf starts producing chlorophyll. “As soon as that happens, Grabosky says, “it becomes its own autonomous unit and starts building itself really quick.” The green leaves spend the spring and summer capturing sunlight and making sugars. The days eventually grow shorter, the tree starts reclaiming nutrients, chlorophyll breaks down and the other colors get their turn.
So the next time you pass a wall of red maples or golden oaks, take a closer look. Fall foliage isn’t just decoration. It’s the visible result of trees responding to light, temperature and their environment while recycling nutrients and preparing for another season. And you don’t need to make a special trip to appreciate the foliage. As Grabosky says, “just get outside and enjoy one leaf at a time.”

articles.title: Welcome to the Season of the Witch! These 13 Facts About Witches Will Completely Captivate You
articles.content:
Every Halloween, witches come out of the woodwork—or, rather, fly in on their broomsticks. They’re on our screens, perched on our porches and roaming the streets in pointy hats, usually with a plastic cauldron full of candy in hand. But witches aren’t just the stuff of Halloween costumes and scary stories. They have a long, complicated history in the real world and an absolutely spellbinding place in pop culture. Think you know everything there is to know about them? Witch, please—there’s a lot to unpack.
We’re stirring up some of the most fascinating facts about witches, witchcraft and more. How many Americans actually believe in witches? More than you might think! Which Swedish holiday features its own witches? Trust us—you won’t guess. And how did centuries of witchcraft, folklore and superstition give us the witches we know today?
From real-life history to Hollywood magic, we’re spilling all the witchy tea ahead.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more entertainment, history, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Across time and around the world, people have been (forgive us) spellbound by witches. Enchanting sorceresses appear in folklore, fairy tales and mythology, but also on stage and screen. Far from the stuff of fiction, about 1 in 4 Americans think witches are real, according to a 2025 Gallup poll.
Witches are real, in that some people practice modern paganism, which includes Wicca and other nature-inspired belief systems. There may be as many as 1.5 million witches in the United States. Maine has the highest percentage of people identifying as “Pagan or Wiccan,” at 4%, per the Pew Research Center. Traditions vary, but these witches are more likely to celebrate the changing seasons than to cast hexes on you.
In the late 1400s, most Europeans believed witchcraft was pure evil—and that witches were in league with the devil himself. Their alleged activities included cursing those they didn’t like, turning people into animals and eating babies. These stories traveled to the New World along with the colonists who began to arrive there, sparking witch trials on both continents.
Historians say 100,000 people were prosecuted as witches in Europe and the Americas from the 1400s to the 1700s. Most were women, but in countries such as Iceland, Estonia and Russia, men made up the majority of those charged. There’s little evidence that any ofthe accused actually practiced witchcraft, though they were often pressured (or tortured) into false confessions.
America’s most notorious witch trial was in Salem, Massachusetts, in the 1690s. (Coincidentally, the final U.S. witchcraft trial was also in Salem, in 1878.) The town has embraced its history and is now a tourist destination that welcomed more than 1 million visitors last October alone. If you go, you can wander through the Salem Witch Museum, pop into countless magic stores or participate in a make-your-own-broomstick workshop.
In L. Frank Baum’s 1900 classic, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Wicked Witch of the West carries an umbrella rather than a broomstick. There’s no mention of her skin being green in the book, but for the 1939 film adaptation, she was given her signature hue to showcase recent advances in Technicolor cinematography. Actor Margaret Hamilton was coated in toxic copper-based paint daily, and her skin was still tinted green for weeks after filming ended.
Take Glinda the Good Witch, who graces Oz looking more like a princess in her sparkly dress and crown. Or Hermione Granger, the main heroine of the Harry Potter series, who’s as smart as she is brave. Historians say 100,000 people were prosecuted as witches in Europe and the Americas from the 1400s to the 1700s. articles.title: Skip the Pumpkin Patch—This Is the Best Place to Buy Pumpkins This Fall
articles.content:
Fall is here, and farmers all over the country are throwing open their barn doors, welcoming the public and inviting them to drop a small fortune on pumpkins. It’s a crafty strategy. After the pumpkin patch, you might as well pick a few apples, and why not have a wagon ride while you’re at it? Before you know it, you’ve spent major bills, and the pumpkins are going to be compost in a month.
While those adorable pictures of your kids in gingham and denim might make it all worth it, sometimes you just need a few pumpkins with no strings attached. We’ve got you covered. Coming up, we have the best place to buy affordable pumpkins this fall, including heirloom pumpkins and jumbo carving pumpkins, with no extra pressure to take a hay ride.
So where is this magical place? Hint: You’re probably already headed there this weekend. Read on for all the details.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, shopping, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
View this post on Instagram
It’s Costco! Yep, pumpkins are back this fall, and compared to the pumpkin patch, they are dirt cheap (just like those Costco pumpkin pies). And we’re not just talking about little baby pumpkins, though they have those too. These are big ones, perfect for carving, as well as heirloom pumpkins, those gorgeous, old-fashioned-looking pumpkins that have been cultivated from the same seed line for decades.
Here’s how the pumpkin prices at Costco break down, though they may vary slightly by location. These are all priced per piece, not by weight, so feel free to grab the biggest one you want.
People are all over social media bragging about their great Costco pumpkins. Here are a few happy customers:
“Our pumpkin is perfect 🎃 I got it [at] Costco for 7 bucks 😝,” someone said on Instagram. “Now let’s see how long it takes for the squirrels to start carving it 🐿️”
“I’d love to support pumpkin patches, but last time we went out one pumpkin that felt like a decent size was $35!! And the smaller one $20,” according to a pumpkin buyer on Reddit.
“I bought a huge pumpkin 🎃 from Costco today … it was only $8,” said a Costco shopper on Facebook.
They’re a lot less. Pumpkin patches generally price their pumpkins by the pound, and some charge an entry fee, which could be $20 or more per person just to get in the gates.
As for the pumpkins, I found one patch in upstate New York that charges 69 cents per pound. Another, in the New York City area, prices them at 79 cents per pound! Conversely, a pumpkin patch in Fort Worth, Texas, charges a $15 entry fee but offers flat pumpkin prices of $3 to $15. Buy two or three, and you’re already over $50.
Costco doesn’t advertise how much their pumpkins weigh, so we can’t make an exact pumpkin-to-pumpkin comparison, but for a fairly typical 25-pound pumpkin, at 79 cents a pound you’re looking at $19.75 for one jack-o’-lantern. Compare that to $7 or $8 bucks at Costco, depending on where you live, and the difference is considerable.
Not really, unless you have a bad back. These jumbo pumpkins are massive, and the heirlooms aren’t tiny either. If it’s pumpkin-buying time in your household, it’s probably a good idea to bring an extra set of muscles—your partner, a friend or your most strapping kid—instead of going it alone.
Other than that, it’s important to choose your pumpkins wisely. Make sure they don’t have any soft spots that might make them rot prematurely, and never pick up a pumpkin by the stem. If it rips off or weakens, you’ve now got an entry point for moisture and decay. Grab them underneath, and don’t forget to bend at the knees.
Costco’s pumpkins are a seasonal item, so they won’t be on sale forever. But you can expect to find them until Halloween or shortly after. Costco’s pumpkins are sourced from the U.S., Canada and Mexico, and the pumpkin-growing season lasts deep into fall. But if you’ve ever made a desperate run to Costco for something only to find it was sold out (temporarily or permanently), your best bet is to stock up well before you buy your Halloween candy.

articles.title: Do Nice Guys (and Gals) Really Finish Last? Here’s What the Science Actually Says
articles.content:
Oh, you are so nice! I used to consider being “nice” as the ultimate compliment. I wanted to be the kind of person that people described as nice, even when I wasn’t in the room.
Which brings me to one of my favorite employment stories: My boss needed help getting a bunch of shifts covered during a very busy season, and I volunteered. Because I’m a team player! Because I genuinely like helping people! And, if I’m being completely honest, because I thought if I was just nice enough, I could get on her good side and get promoted.
For months, I burned myself out, working early and late shifts on top of my own workload. Then one day, I finally got an email from my boss. I assumed it was going to be something like: “Thank you so much for all the extra work you’ve been putting in. I couldn’t do this without you!” Nope. Instead, she scolded me for not cleaning enough after one shift and ended with the line: “Don’t forget—working here is a privilege.” My brain exploded.
Y’all, it was a minimum-wage job.
I was not working as a peacekeeper for the U.N. I was not curing childhood cancer. I was not following the president around with a briefcase of nuclear codes handcuffed to my wrist. And the truth was that I was doing her a favor for basically the price of a cup of coffee (and my dignity)!
Not only did being nice not get me a promotion—it didn’t even get me recognized as a good human being. But the part that stung the worst? The person who did get the promotion was the definition of Not Nice. It was one of the moments where you start to understand why people say nice guys finish last. (Or in my case, nice gals work 50 extra shifts, clean the bathroom, organize the equipment, get an ulcer and then apologize for leaving some boxes out … because that’s what I did.)
But still, being nice is a good thing, right? We see how awesome it can be time and again in Reader’s Digest‘s annual Nicest Places in America search. And let’s be honest: No one wants to hang out with (or date) a jerk. But do nice guys really finish last? It turns out that science does have an answer, but it’s complicated. And it starts with defining what “nice” really is.
Read on to find out what actually qualifies as being nice and what it can lead to—if you do it the right way.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more life tips, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
For starters, “nice” doesn’t mean being a doormat, says Adam Mendler, PhD, who teaches graduate-level leadership courses at UCLA and hosts the Thirty Minute Mentors podcast, where he regularly advises people on how to be both nice and successful. “Kindness can signal to people that you’re soft or a pushover,” he says. “Some people will try to see how far they can push you or what they can get away with.”
Eliska Kostelny, PsyD, a licensed clinical professional counselor and clinical supervisor at Pure Health Center, adds another concern to the mix: “Being nice” can be seen as not being proactive or passionate.
OK, so what does it really mean to be nice? The word is actually so nebulous and used in so many different contexts—good and bad—that researchers often avoid it, says Christian Bumpous, a licensed psychotherapist and the founder of Therapie in Nashville.
So instead of researching niceness, scientists instead tend to look at “agreeableness,” a Big Five trait that includes trust, straightforwardness, altruism, compliance, modesty and tender-mindedness—or “kindness,” which the Kindlab defines as “an action intended to benefit someone else at some cost to yourself.”
It depends entirely on the setting. When people talk about nice guys finishing last, it’s usually in the context of pay/promotions at work, love and overall happiness. And the answer changes depending on which one of those three things you’re measuring. For instance, the agreeable type of “nice” is sometimes linked with poorer work outcomes, while true kindness is linked to more successful relationships, better reputations and increased well-being. Here’s how it breaks down.
In a classic study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, researchers found that overall agreeable people do earn less over the course of their careers—and the effect was stronger for men. “The researchers assumed it was likely because they negotiate and advocate for themselves less than less-nice peers,” Bumpous says. “A person can end up avoiding conflict and saying yes too often. They tend to undernegotiate and get overlooked for raises and promotions at work. Over time, that can build resentment, which in turn leads to increased stress and feelings of burnout.”
However, while the research focuses on agreeableness, Mendler says that kindness produces different results because people who are kind are likable. “People would rather work with, hire, promote and support someone they like and trust,” he says. “Over the years, I have been given opportunities I wasn’t the best candidate for because the decision-maker liked me, and a big part of being likable is being kind.”
Research backs that up: A study published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin found that strangers placed in random groups were most likely to choose the most altruistic group members to be both leaders and partners. So if your work involves leadership or working with others, being kind is a must.
“Kindness leads to stronger trust in relationships, more loyalty, and increased social support,” Bumpous says. “All three things can be protective factors that ultimately buffer stress. It also leads to better teamwork and a better reputation at work over time.”
Despite what the internet may tell you, kind men are not finishing last in love. In fact, it’s quite the opposite. A foundational study published in 2003 found that women prefer men who come across as kind and sensitive over those who are jerks—even when the jerk was rated as more attractive. A follow-up study of 191 male college students found that men who scored lower in agreeableness were more likely to have casual, less-committed sexual relationships. So if you’re looking for real romance, being nice is the way to go.
Bumpous references the decades of research on relationships done by the Gottman Institute: “They found kindness is one of the strongest predictors when it comes to stable partnerships. In the long run, being nice works out.”
Of course, romance is only one type of relationship, and a fulfilling life has many types of close connections. “We also often see the ‘nice guy’ archetype as the unrequited, friend-zoned person who is overlooked by their romantic interest, who instead pursues the ‘bad boy,’” Kostelny says. “In reality, truly nice people rarely finish last, because they are more likely to create community and friendships that result in life satisfaction.”
Nice people are happier. Why? The primary driver of happiness is meaningful relationships, according to the Harvard Longevity Study, the longest-running study on happiness in the world. “Typically, kind people tend to be happier and can form more durable friendships, and they also have stronger romantic relationships,” Bumpous says. “Overall, kindness is linked to higher well-being for the person who’s being kind.”
It is also true that being kind—as in selflessly helping someone else—has been linked over and over in the research to more feelings of happiness. In a 2018 meta-analysis that reviewed 27 experiments involving more than 4,000 people, researchers found that people who performed acts of kindness reported significantly higher well-being than those who didn’t.
Usually not, but the ones who do tend to be either pushovers or are being performatively nice. The latter is when people are being kind … but also looking to get something out of it vs. doing it selflessly. Looking back at my experience, I can see now that I was being both a pushover and performatively nice. So perhaps it’s not surprising that I didn’t get the result I was looking for. But when you’re looking at success, it’s important to play the long game.
“In the short term, aggressive or selfish behavior can pay off, making it look like the nice guy finished last, but in the long run, your reputation catches up with you,” Mendler says. “People remember who treated them well, who treated them poorly and who was only nice when they wanted something.”
Yes, but it’s mostly in how they’re judged by other people, not in how nice they actually are. “There is a definite difference in expectations,” Mendler says. “Aggressive and assertive behavior is often rewarded in men and penalized in women.” He explains that a man who pushes hard may be viewed as strong, while a woman who behaves the same way may be viewed as difficult.
Women are also generally expected to be more accommodating and conflict-averse. As a result, women in the workplace can be looked down on both for being too soft and for not being soft enough. “It is a double standard that many well-meaning people are not aware of,” he says.
But men can be negatively affected by these stereotypes as well. “On the flip side, nice men can be seen as less dominant or soft,’ so both genders can get punished,” Bumpous says. “It just shows up in different ways.”
It’s about being kind while also having boundaries—and those boundaries need to be nonnegotiable. Now, it’s important to say that setting limits does not mean you’re being mean. “A kind person helps because they want to,” Mendler explains. “A pushover helps because they don’t feel comfortable saying no.”
Bumpous adds that kindness paired with self-respect, self-awareness of your boundaries and honesty about what you can and cannot do—and being assertive about it—is the magic formula. Kostelny adds: “Contrary to popular belief, a person can be both nice and ambitious. The important thing is to lift yourself up at the same time you are lifting others.”
Here’s how to make it work.
Looking back, I can now see that what I thought of as “being nice” was actually an early-ingrained trauma response that turned me into a nuclear-level people pleaser. I didn’t just want people to like me. I wanted to be so useful that nobody would ever have a reason to be mad at me. Essentially, I had confused being useful with being worthy.
At the time, it felt devastating. I had followed all the rules I thought I was supposed to follow. I worked hard. I helped. I stayed late. I said yes. I made myself indispensable. And I thought if I gave enough of myself away, eventually somebody would look at me and say, “You’ve done enough. You deserve something too.”
Instead, I got a cleaning complaint.
Being nice doesn’t mean saying yes to everything. Being kind doesn’t mean abandoning yourself. And making yourself indispensable is an awful way to find out whether someone actually values you.
These days, I’m still nice. But it’s because I want to be, not because I need to prove it to someone else.

We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. For this piece on whether nice guys finish last, Charlotte Hilton Andersen tapped her experience as a longtime journalist who frequently writes about psychology, communication, etiquette and common curiosities for Reader’s Digest. I assumed it was going to be something like: “Thank you so much for all the extra work you’ve been putting in. I couldn’t do this without you!” Nope. Instead, she scolded me for not cleaning enough after one shift and ended with the line: “Don’t forget—working here is a privilege.” My brain exploded.

Y’all, it was a minimum-wage job. 

I was not working as a peacekeeper for the U.N. I was not curing childhood cancer. I was not following the president around with a briefcase of nuclear codes handcuffed to my wrist. And the truth was that I was doing her a favor for basically the price of a cup of coffee (and my dignity)!

Not only did being nice not get me a promotion—it didn’t even get me recognized as a good human being. But the part that stung the worst? The person who did get the promotion was the definition of Not Nice. It was one of the moments where you start to understand why people say nice guys finish last. (Or in my case, nice gals work 50 extra shifts, clean the bathroom, organize the equipment, get an ulcer and then apologize for leaving some boxes out … because that’s what I did.)

But still, being nice is a good thing, right? We see how awesome it can be time and again in Reader’s Digest‘s annual Nicest Places in America search. And let’s be honest: No one wants to hang out with (or date) a jerk. But do nice guys really finish last? It turns out that science does have an answer, but it’s complicated. And it starts with defining what “nice” really is.

Read on to find out what actually qualifies as being nice and what it can lead to—if you do it the right way.

What does it mean to be “nice”?

For starters, “nice” doesn’t mean being a doormat, says Adam Mendler, PhD, who teaches graduate-level leadership courses at UCLA and hosts the Thirty Minute Mentors podcast, where he regularly advises people on how to be both nice and successful. “Kindness can signal to people that you’re soft or a pushover,” he says. “Some people will try to see how far they can push you or what they can get away with.”  

Eliska Kostelny, PsyD, a licensed clinical professional counselor and clinical supervisor at Pure Health Center, adds another concern to the mix: “Being nice” can be seen as not being proactive or passionate.

OK, so what does it really mean to be nice? The word is actually so nebulous and used in so many different contexts—good and bad—that researchers often avoid it, says Christian Bumpous, a licensed psychotherapist and the founder of Therapie in Nashville. 

So instead of researching niceness, scientists instead tend to look at “agreeableness,” a Big Five trait that includes trust, straightforwardness, altruism, compliance, modesty and tender-mindedness—or “kindness,” which the Kindlab defines as “an action intended to benefit someone else at some cost to yourself.”

What does the research show about being nice?

It depends entirely on the setting. When people talk about nice guys finishing last, it’s usually in the context of pay/promotions at work, love and overall happiness. And the answer changes depending on which one of those three things you’re measuring. For instance, the agreeable type of “nice” is sometimes linked with poorer work outcomes, while true kindness is linked to more successful relationships, better reputations and increased well-being. Here’s how it breaks down.

Work

In a classic study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, researchers found that overall agreeable people do earn less over the course of their careers—and the effect was stronger for men. “The researchers assumed it was likely because they negotiate and advocate for themselves less than less-nice peers,” Bumpous says. “A person can end up avoiding conflict and saying yes too often. They tend to undernegotiate and get overlooked for raises and promotions at work. Over time, that can build resentment, which in turn leads to increased stress and feelings of burnout.” 

However, while the research focuses on agreeableness, Mendler says that kindness produces different results because people who are kind are likable. “People would rather work with, hire, promote and support someone they like and trust,” he says. “Over the years, I have been given opportunities I wasn’t the best candidate for because the decision-maker liked me, and a big part of being likable is being kind.”

Research backs that up: A study published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin found that strangers placed in random groups were most likely to choose the most altruistic group members to be both leaders and partners. So if your work involves leadership or working with others, being kind is a must. 

“Kindness leads to stronger trust in relationships, more loyalty, and increased social support,” Bumpous says. “All three things can be protective factors that ultimately buffer stress. It also leads to better teamwork and a better reputation at work over time.”

Love and friendship

Despite what the internet may tell you, kind men are not finishing last in love. In fact, it’s quite the opposite. A foundational study published in 2003 found that women prefer men who come across as kind and sensitive over those who are jerks—even when the jerk was rated as more attractive. A follow-up study of 191 male college students found that men who scored lower in agreeableness were more likely to have casual, less-committed sexual relationships. So if you’re looking for real romance, being nice is the way to go.

Bumpous references the decades of research on relationships done by the Gottman Institute: “They found kindness is one of the strongest predictors when it comes to stable partnerships. In the long run, being nice works out.”

Of course, romance is only one type of relationship, and a fulfilling life has many types of close connections. “We also often see the ‘nice guy’ archetype as the unrequited, friend-zoned person who is overlooked by their romantic interest, who instead pursues the ‘bad boy,’” Kostelny says. “In reality, truly nice people rarely finish last, because they are more likely to create community and friendships that result in life satisfaction.”

Happiness and well-being

Nice people are happier. Why? The primary driver of happiness is meaningful relationships, according to the Harvard Longevity Study, the longest-running study on happiness in the world. “Typically, kind people tend to be happier and can form more durable friendships, and they also have stronger romantic relationships,” Bumpous says. “Overall, kindness is linked to higher well-being for the person who’s being kind.”

It is also true that being kind—as in selflessly helping someone else—has been linked over and over in the research to more feelings of happiness. In a 2018 meta-analysis that reviewed 27 experiments involving more than 4,000 people, researchers found that people who performed acts of kindness reported significantly higher well-being than those who didn’t.

So do nice guys actually finish last?

Usually not, but the ones who do tend to be either pushovers or are being performatively nice. The latter is when people are being kind … but also looking to get something out of it vs. doing it selflessly. Looking back at my experience, I can see now that I was being both a pushover and performatively nice. So perhaps it’s not surprising that I didn’t get the result I was looking for. But when you’re looking at success, it’s important to play the long game. 

“In the short term, aggressive or selfish behavior can pay off, making it look like the nice guy finished last, but in the long run, your reputation catches up with you,” Mendler says. “People remember who treated them well, who treated them poorly and who was only nice when they wanted something.”

Is there a difference between nice guys and nice girls?

Yes, but it’s mostly in how they’re judged by other people, not in how nice they actually are. “There is a definite difference in expectations,” Mendler says. “Aggressive and assertive behavior is often rewarded in men and penalized in women.” He explains that a man who pushes hard may be viewed as strong, while a woman who behaves the same way may be viewed as difficult.

Women are also generally expected to be more accommodating and conflict-averse. As a result, women in the workplace can be looked down on both for being too soft and for not being soft enough. “It is a double standard that many well-meaning people are not aware of,” he says. 

But men can be negatively affected by these stereotypes as well. “On the flip side, nice men can be seen as less dominant or soft,’ so both genders can get punished,” Bumpous says. “It just shows up in different ways.”

How can you be nice without being a pushover?

It’s about being kind while also having boundaries—and those boundaries need to be nonnegotiable. Now, it’s important to say that setting limits does not mean you’re being mean. “A kind person helps because they want to,” Mendler explains. “A pushover helps because they don’t feel comfortable saying no.”

Bumpous adds that kindness paired with self-respect, self-awareness of your boundaries and honesty about what you can and cannot do—and being assertive about it—is the magic formula. Kostelny adds: “Contrary to popular belief, a person can be both nice and ambitious. The important thing is to lift yourself up at the same time you are lifting others.”

Here’s how to make it work.

  • Run the “Did I truly choose this?” test. Bumpous explains that “a ‘yes’ from a pushover comes from fear and not necessarily choice. It’s helpful to ask yourself, ‘Did I truly choose this? Or was I afraid of the reaction if I said no?’ Feeling resentment after saying yes is a big clue.”
  • Ask yourself what your motive is. Mendler says that “if someone asks too much of you and you still agree because you’re afraid of upsetting them, you’re being a pushover. If someone treats you poorly and you allow it to continue because you want to avoid conflict, you’re being a pushover. You can be generous and magnanimous without giving other people control over you.”
  • Learn to say no (without a five-paragraph apology). “No” is a complete sentence, and it can also be a kind one. “The idea is you can say no without overexplaining, give without keeping score and check in with yourself: What do you have capacity for?” Bumpous says.
  • Be honest about what you need. You can be nice and still be more assertive, confidently expressing your needs while being open to listen to, understand and compromise with others. “The important thing is to practice both kindness and self-advocacy in these roles when working toward specific goals,” Kostelny says.
  • Set boundaries. A boundary is simply stating you will do X if Y happens. It’s not about changing the other person’s behavior; it’s about your reaction to it. “If you don’t set boundaries, favors can quickly become expectations, and some people will keep taking until you stop giving,” Mendel says. Which, by the way, is exactly what happened in my job.

So what should you really take away from all of this?

Looking back, I can now see that what I thought of as “being nice” was actually an early-ingrained trauma response that turned me into a nuclear-level people pleaser. I didn’t just want people to like me. I wanted to be so useful that nobody would ever have a reason to be mad at me. Essentially, I had confused being useful with being worthy. 

At the time, it felt devastating. I had followed all the rules I thought I was supposed to follow. I worked hard. I helped. I stayed late. I said yes. I made myself indispensable. And I thought if I gave enough of myself away, eventually somebody would look at me and say, “You’ve done enough. You deserve something too.” 

Instead, I got a cleaning complaint. 

Being nice doesn’t mean saying yes to everything. Being kind doesn’t mean abandoning yourself. And making yourself indispensable is an awful way to find out whether someone actually values you.

These days, I’m still nice. But it’s because I want to be, not because I need to prove it to someone else.
